chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan, from Is'haq ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a man who performs Hajj and dedicates his Hajj and Umrah, or part of his circumambulation, for one of his family members, while he is absent from him in another city. I said, 'Will that reduce his reward?' He said, 'No. It is for him and for his companion, and for him is a reward besides that with what he has linked.' I said, 'And if he is deceased, does that enter upon him?' He said, 'Yes, to the extent that if he is under Wrath, it is forgiven for him, or if there is constriction upon him, it is expanded upon him.' I said, 'So he, in his place, knows that that deed has reached him?' He said, 'Yes.' I said, 'And even if he was a Nasibi (hostile one), does that benefit him?' He said, 'Yes. It is lightened from him.'

key_terms.نَاصِب: Nasibi (one hostile to the Ahl al-Bayt)

ai.seo_question: Can a living person perform Hajj on behalf of a deceased relative and share the reward?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies that dedicating Hajj or Umrah to absent or deceased relatives is valid, with the reward shared between the performer and the dedicatee. It further establishes that these acts can alleviate punishment or expand one's standing in the afterlife, even for those hostile to the Ahl al-Bayt, demonstrating the universal efficacy of ritual devotion in Shia jurisprudence.
